reference.source: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
clinicalPearls: The most common benign neoplasm of the larynx, caused by human papillomavirus, chiefly types 6 and 11
It occurs in a juvenile form, typically multiple and more aggressive, and an adult form that is often more localised
The usual presentation is progressive hoarseness or a weak or abnormal cry in a child, and with growth it can cause stridor and airway obstruction
Juvenile disease is thought to be acquired through vertical transmission from maternal genital HPV infection during birth
Laryngoscopy shows soft, warty, exophytic lesions favouring the vocal cords and other sites of squamous-ciliary junction
Because there is no definitive cure, treatment centres on repeated conservative surgical removal (commonly microlaryngeal or laser) to maintain the airway and voice while preserving normal tissue
The disease is characterised by frequent recurrence and can spread down the tracheobronchial tree, and a tracheostomy is best avoided as it may promote distal spread
Malignant transformation is uncommon but recognised, particularly with certain HPV types or after irradiation, so persistent or atypical lesions warrant biopsy
reference.pathophysiology: Laryngeal papillomatosis results from infection of the respiratory epithelium by human papillomavirus, most often types 6 and 11, which drives proliferation of squamous epithelium into finger-like papillary fronds supported by fibrovascular cores. Lesions favour the transition zones between squamous and ciliary epithelium, so the vocal cords are commonly affected. In children the virus is usually acquired at birth from an infected maternal genital tract, and the immature or immunologically naive host tends to develop multiple, recurrent lesions. Latent virus in adjacent normal-looking mucosa underlies the persistent recurrence after removal, and lesions may seed distally in the airway.
additionalDifferentials: Croup or other infective laryngitis in a child
additionalInvestigations: Flexible and rigid laryngoscopy to identify and map the papillomas
Microlaryngoscopy under anaesthesia for detailed assessment and tissue removal
Histopathology of excised tissue to confirm the diagnosis and exclude dysplasia or malignancy
HPV typing where available, as certain types carry higher risk
Airway assessment for distal (tracheobronchial) spread in aggressive disease
redFlags: Progressive stridor and airway obstruction from bulky laryngeal disease requiring urgent airway management
Distal spread into the trachea and bronchi indicating aggressive disease
Features suggesting malignant transformation such as a firm, ulcerated, or rapidly enlarging lesion
Rapid recurrence needing frequent surgical intervention
reference.prognosis: The course is unpredictable and marked by recurrence; juvenile disease may require many procedures over years before eventual regression around puberty in some children, while adult disease is often more limited, and although malignant change is rare it is an important long-term consideration.
pitfalls: Aggressive surgery that damages the vocal cords and causes scarring or web formation
Performing a tracheostomy that may encourage distal tracheobronchial spread
Assuming benignity and not biopsying atypical or persistent lesions
Overlooking airway compromise in a child presenting only with a hoarse cry
references: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
